chapters.title: Chapter 3: Reading and Building a Cap Table

lessons.title: Convertibles on the Cap Table: How Notes and iSAFEs Convert

children.text: Many Indian startups raise their first outside money without ever agreeing a valuation. Angels sign an iSAFE, a family office writes a convertible note, and everyone agrees to "figure out the price at the next round". Those instruments are easy to forget because they are not ordinary shares yet. But when a Series A closes, they turn into shares in one go, and they can take a surprisingly large bite out of everyone's ownership. This lesson shows how they convert and how to put them on a cap table before they surprise you.

body.text: A convertible is a cap table entry with the number of shares left blank. The blank gets filled in at the next priced round, using a discount, a valuation cap or both, and whoever did not model it in advance is the one who gets diluted.

children.text: The Two Instruments You Will Meet in India

columns.label: Convertible note
points: Starts as debt: money the startup owes the holder
Exempt from deposit rules only for DPIIT-recognised startups raising at least ₹25 lakh in a single tranche
Must convert into equity or be repaid within 10 years
Can carry interest, which usually converts along with the principal
Can be issued to foreign investors under FEMA, subject to conditions

columns.label: iSAFE
points: India Simple Agreement for Future Equity, adapted from the US SAFE
Structured as CCPS, so it is share capital from day one, not debt
No repayment obligation and no interest
Converts into equity shares at the next priced round

children.text: Some startups also use
compulsorily convertible debentures
(CCDs). Whatever the legal form, the cap table question is the same: how many shares will this become, and when?

markDefs.definition: Debentures that must convert into equity shares at a set time or event. Like CCPS, they count as equity instruments for foreign investment purposes.

body.label: Why a plain US SAFE does not work in India
body.context: A US-style SAFE is a contract for future shares with no share issued today. Indian company law and FEMA pricing rules fit poorly with that structure, which is why Indian versions like the iSAFE are issued as CCPS with the conversion terms written in.

children.text: The Two Terms That Decide Your Shares
Because convertible holders take the most risk by investing before a price is set, they get a better price than the next round's investors. Two terms deliver that.
Discount.
The holder converts at a percentage below the round price. A 20% discount on a ₹400 round price means converting at ₹320.
[[Valuation cap|The maximum valuation at which a convertible converts. If the next round is priced above the cap, the holder converts as if the round were priced at the cap.]].
The holder converts at no higher than the price implied by the cap. A ₹10 crore cap on 10,00,000 shares means converting at no more than ₹100.

body.latex: \text{Conversion price} = \min\left(\text{Round price} \times (1 - \text{Discount}),\ \frac{\text{Valuation cap}}{\text{Fully diluted shares before the round}}\right)
body.caption: The holder gets whichever price is lower, and therefore more shares

body.latex: \text{Conversion shares} = \frac{\text{Amount converting (principal plus any accrued interest)}}{\text{Conversion price}}
body.caption: The blank on the cap table, filled in

body.text: Definitions vary between documents. Some caps are measured on a share count that includes the convertibles themselves or a new ESOP pool, which changes the cap price. Always read how the instrument defines the share count before you calculate anything.

children.text: Worked Example: LoomLink Raises Its Series A

LoomLink Textiles Tech Private Limited is a fictional Coimbatore startup that connects small power-loom owners with garment exporters. Before its Series A it has 10,00,000 fully diluted shares: 9,00,000 held by founders and a 1,00,000-share ESOP pool. It also has two convertibles outstanding.

cells: ₹1.12 crore (₹1 crore plus ₹12 lakh accrued interest)

children.text: The Series A investor puts in ₹12 crore at a ₹40 crore pre-money valuation, so the round price is ₹40 crore ÷ 10,00,000 = ₹400. The 20% discount price is ₹320 for both instruments.

body.caption: Converting each instrument at the Series A
LoomLink cap table after Series A (fully diluted)

children.text: Percentages are rounded and add up to 99.99%. Conversion shares are rounded down to whole shares.

body.text: In this simple version, the conversion shares dilute everyone, including the Series A investor. That is why Series A investors often push for conversion shares to be counted inside the pre-money share count, just like an ESOP pool shuffle, so that only existing holders bear them. The maths then becomes circular, because the round price depends on the share count and the conversion shares depend on the round price, and it is usually solved inside the term sheet model.

children.text: Cap or Discount: Which One Wins?
The cap protects the holder when the next round is priced high. The discount protects them when it is priced low. Here is what the angels' ₹50 lakh iSAFE converts into at different Series A prices.

body.caption: iSAFE conversion at different round prices (₹10 crore cap, 20% discount)

body.title: Value of the angels' ₹50 lakh iSAFE at conversion

children.text: Below a ₹125 round price, the discount guarantees the holder 25% more value than they put in: ₹50 lakh ÷ 0.8 = ₹62.5 lakh. Above ₹125, the cap takes over and every extra rupee of round price flows straight to the holder. An iSAFE with no cap only ever gets the discount, however well the company does.

body.title: Convert an iSAFE
body.prompt: You hold a ₹25 lakh iSAFE with a ₹12 crore valuation cap and a 20% discount. The startup has 8,00,000 fully diluted shares before its Series A, which is priced at ₹250 per share. How many shares do you receive? Round to the nearest whole share.
body.explanation: Discount price = ₹250 × 0.8 = ₹200. Cap price = ₹12 crore ÷ 8,00,000 = ₹150. The lower price, ₹150, applies. Shares = ₹25 lakh ÷ ₹150 = 16,666.67, which rounds to 16,667. In practice most documents round down, which would give 16,666.

body.title: When does the discount win?
body.question: A convertible has a ₹20 crore cap on 10,00,000 shares and a 20% discount. At which Series A price does the discount give the holder a better price than the cap?
body.explanation: The cap price is ₹20 crore ÷ 10,00,000 = ₹200. The discount beats the cap only when round price × 0.8 is below ₹200, which means a round price below ₹250. At ₹200, the discount price is ₹160, better than the ₹200 cap price. At ₹250 the two are equal, and at ₹275 or ₹300 the cap wins.

body.title: The upside protector
body.textWithBlank: The term that limits the price at which a convertible converts, so the holder benefits if the next round is priced high, is called the valuation ___.
body.explanation: The cap sets a ceiling on the conversion price. The discount, by contrast, guarantees a price below the round price whatever the round is priced at.

children.text: The Hidden Cap Table Problem

body.text: Convertibles are often left off the cap table a founder shows you, because "they have not converted yet". A startup can quietly stack three or four iSAFEs and notes with low caps. At Series A, they convert all at once, and a founder who thought they owned 65% can find themselves at 55%, with angels who invested in a priced round diluted just as sharply.

children.text: The fix is a
pro forma cap table
. Ask the founders to show the cap table as it would look after the next round, with every convertible converted at a realistic round price.

markDefs.definition: A cap table showing ownership as it would look after a planned event, such as a funding round with all convertibles converted.

body.title: The uncapped iSAFE offer
body.scenario: A Mumbai creator-economy startup offers you a ₹10 lakh iSAFE with a 15% discount and no valuation cap. The founder says: "No cap is cleaner, and we expect to raise a big Series A within 18 months." You also learn they have already issued ₹1.5 crore of iSAFEs to other angels at a ₹15 crore cap.
body.prompt: Should you accept an uncapped iSAFE? What else should the existing ₹1.5 crore of iSAFEs make you think about?
body.modelAnswer:
On the uncapped iSAFE:
1. Without a cap, your only reward for early risk is a 15% discount. If the Series A is priced very high, you convert at 85% of that high price, taking early-stage risk for a late-stage price.
2. Other angels already have a ₹15 crore cap. If the Series A is priced well above ₹15 crore, they convert at a far better price than you on the same instrument type.
3. Ask for the same ₹15 crore cap and a comparable discount, or pass.

On the existing ₹1.5 crore of iSAFEs:
1. At a ₹15 crore cap they convert into roughly 10% of the pre-round share count, before counting your own iSAFE, any new ESOP pool or the Series A money.
2. Ask for a pro forma cap table after a realistic Series A, with every convertible converted.
3. Check whether the Series A investor is likely to insist that conversion shares sit in the pre-money, which would push the dilution onto founders and existing holders.
4. Confirm all outstanding convertibles, including any family or friends notes, are disclosed in writing.

body.title: Questions to ask about any convertible
steps: Is it a convertible note, iSAFE (CCPS) or CCD, and has it been properly issued and filed?
What is the valuation cap, and on exactly which share count is the cap price calculated?
Does interest accrue, and does it convert along with the principal?
What triggers conversion: a qualified round of a minimum size, a sale, a maturity date?
For a convertible note: what happens at maturity if no round has taken place?
Are conversion shares counted in the pre-money or post-money of the next round?
Can I see a pro forma cap table with every convertible converted?

cards.definition: Debt that converts into equity at a later round. In India, used by DPIIT-recognised startups for amounts of at least ₹25 lakh in a single tranche.
India Simple Agreement for Future Equity: an early-stage instrument issued as CCPS that converts into equity at the next priced round.
The maximum valuation at which a convertible converts, protecting the holder if the next round is priced high.
A percentage reduction on the next round's price at which a convertible converts.
The lower of the discounted round price and the cap price.
Compulsorily convertible debenture: a debenture that must convert into equity shares.
A cap table showing ownership after a planned round, with all convertibles converted.

points: Convertible notes start as debt. iSAFEs are issued as CCPS. Both become equity shares at the next priced round.
Conversion price is the lower of the discounted round price and the cap price, and holders receive amount ÷ conversion price in shares.
The discount protects holders in low-priced rounds. The cap rewards them in high-priced rounds.
Conversion shares dilute existing holders and, unless placed in the pre-money, the new investor too.
Convertibles are often left off cap tables until they convert. Always ask for a pro forma cap table.
Be wary of uncapped instruments and of stacks of low-cap convertibles ahead of a Series A.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or tax advice. LoomLink and the other startups described are fictional. Convertible instruments vary widely in their terms and in how they are treated under the Companies Act, deposit rules and FEMA. Startup investments are high risk and illiquid. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a lawyer before investing.
